title: The Rupee Just Hit a Record Low. For NRIs, That Changes the Remittance Math.
excerpt: India's currency has lost seven percent since the Iran war began, breaching 96 to the dollar. For the diaspora, it is both a windfall on transfers home and a warning about the economy they left behind.
body:
The Indian rupee closed at a record low of 96.35 against the US dollar on Monday, capping a punishing stretch that has seen the currency lose more than seven percent since the Iran war erupted in late February. With Brent crude above $111 a barrel and the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to commercial shipping, the forces battering the rupee show no sign of relenting.

For the roughly 32 million Indians living abroad, the slide presents a paradox. Every dollar remitted home now converts to more rupees than at any point in history. But the same forces driving that favourable exchange rate — surging oil prices, capital flight, and a widening trade deficit — are quietly eroding the Indian economy that the diaspora remains deeply invested in.

## How We Got Here

The rupee's descent has been relentless. It breached the psychologically significant 96 mark on May 15, when Brent crude touched $109 a barrel and oil marketing companies raised domestic fuel prices by ₹3 per litre. By May 18, it had plunged further to 96.35, with traders citing a toxic combination of surging US Treasury yields (the 10-year hit 4.625 percent), foreign portfolio outflows, and the Reserve Bank of India's dwindling ability to defend the currency.

The RBI has been intervening aggressively, selling dollars from its reserves to slow the slide. But analysts at multiple brokerages estimate the central bank has burned through $25-30 billion in reserves since March, and the intervention is merely managing the pace of decline rather than reversing it. The rupee is now Asia's worst-performing currency in 2026.

The proximate cause is oil. India imports roughly 88 percent of its crude needs, and before the conflict, around 60 percent of that transited the Strait of Hormuz. With the strait blockaded since mid-April, India has pivoted heavily to Russian crude — imports from Moscow hit record highs in early May. But the US sanctions waiver that permitted these purchases expired on May 16, and Washington has not yet confirmed an extension. If the waiver lapses permanently, India faces the prospect of losing its primary replacement supply just as traditional Middle Eastern barrels remain inaccessible.

The current account deficit, which economists at multiple banks now project could reach $65 billion for the fiscal year, is the widest in over a decade. Foreign portfolio investors have pulled billions from Indian equities and bonds since March, adding to the dollar demand that the RBI is struggling to meet.

## The Remittance Paradox

For NRIs, particularly the millions working in the Gulf, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada, the arithmetic of sending money home has never looked better in nominal terms. At 96.35, a $1,000 transfer yields ₹96,350 — roughly ₹10,000 more than it would have a year ago. For families in Kerala, Punjab, and Telangana who depend on monthly remittances, that translates into meaningfully more purchasing power.

Remittance flows to India — which totalled approximately $125 billion in 2025, the highest of any country globally — are expected to rise further in dollar terms as the exchange rate incentivises larger transfers. Several fintech platforms report a surge in remittance volumes since the rupee broke below 95.

But the windfall has a shadow. A weaker rupee also means that the Indian real estate, fixed deposits, and equity portfolios that many NRIs hold back home are worth less in dollar terms. An apartment in Bangalore purchased for ₹1 crore five years ago, when the dollar traded at 83, has lost roughly 16 percent of its dollar value on currency alone — before accounting for any change in the property's rupee price. For NRIs planning an eventual return, the maths of when and how to repatriate savings has become considerably more complex.

## Markets Swing on Iran Hopes

Indian equity markets rallied late on Monday after President Trump announced the cancellation of a planned military strike on Iran. The GIFT Nifty, which allows international investors to trade Indian index futures outside regular hours, jumped sharply on reports that Gulf states had brokered a diplomatic pause. Oil prices slipped from their intra-day highs, with Brent briefly falling below $109 before settling near $110.

But market veterans counsel against premature optimism. SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey, speaking at an industry event last week, said Indian markets had shown "resilience" to the West Asia shock but acknowledged that sustained high oil prices would test that composure. The Sensex has shed roughly 8 percent from its pre-conflict peak, and banking stocks — particularly those exposed to oil-importing corporate borrowers — remain under pressure.

The RBI's record dividend to the government, expected to approach ₹3 lakh crore this year, provides a fiscal cushion. But analysts warn that the dividend reflects profits from the central bank's dollar sales — essentially, the RBI is monetising its reserves to fund the government, a strategy that has clear limits.

## What the Diaspora Should Watch

Three variables will determine whether the rupee stabilises or slides further toward the once-unthinkable 100 mark.

First, the Russian oil waiver. If the US extends General License 134B, India's refiners can keep operating on discounted Russian crude, easing pressure on the import bill and the current account. If it lapses, the scramble for alternative supply will intensify and the rupee will bear the cost.

Second, the Iran diplomacy. Trump's 72-hour window for Gulf-brokered negotiations will either produce a framework for reopening the Strait of Hormuz or collapse into the military escalation he paused. A reopened strait would bring immediate relief to oil prices and, by extension, to the rupee.

Third, the monsoon. A normal monsoon would temper food inflation and reduce the RBI's need to keep interest rates elevated, potentially attracting some foreign capital back. The India Meteorological Department's latest forecast calls for above-normal rainfall, but the season is still weeks away.

For NRIs, the strategic calculus is straightforward: lock in favourable remittance rates now, but hedge against further depreciation on Indian-denominated assets. The rupee's record low is not a floor. It may prove to be a waystation.
